cards.explanation: The answer is the Book of Records. The king "…ordered the Book of Records, the Chronicles, to be brought in and read to him." (Esther 6:1). Xerxes, the king in this story, picked the records. I think that's some of the most sleep-proof reading material around, friends.

The answer is False. The record says Mordecai "…had exposed Bigthana and Teresh, two of the eunuchs who guarded the king’s entrance…" (Esther 6:2). Those two were the ones who had conspired to assassinate the king. Mordecai exposed the plot, and it was all written down.

The answer is nothing. The king asks what honor Mordecai received, and the attendants reply, "Nothing has been done for him…" (Esther 6:3). Mordecai saved the king's life, and the thank-you card never got written. I think the king is about to fix that, friends.

The answer is Haman. The attendants say, "Haman is there, standing in the court." (Esther 6:5). He'd just walked in to ask the king to hang Mordecai. Of every person who could be standing there right now, it's him. The timing is unreal, bakers.

The answer is True. The text says Haman "…had just entered the outer court of the palace to ask the king to hang Mordecai on the gallows he had prepared for him." (Esther 6:4). He came with his request already in hand. Meanwhile the king has Mordecai on his mind too, just for a very different reason.

The answer is True. The text says Haman thought to himself, “Whom would the king be delighted to honor more than me?” (Esther 6:6). He heard “…the man whom the king is delighted to honor?” and figured it was him. That sets up the surprise, friends.

The two words are worn and ridden. The robe is one "…the king himself has worn…" (Esther 6:8), and the horse is one "…on which the king himself has ridden…" (Esther 6:8), wearing a royal crest on its head. Haman didn't ask for a nice new robe off the rack. He wanted the king's own, and he was aiming high, friends.

The answer is one of the king's most noble princes. Haman says, "Let the robe and the horse be entrusted to one of the king’s most noble princes." (Esther 6:9). That prince dresses the honored man and parades him through the city square. Haman is picturing a very classy parade, friends.

The answer is False. In Haman's plan the man is paraded "…through the city square, proclaiming before him, ‘This is what is done for the man whom the king is delighted to honor!’…" (Esther 6:9). There's no quiet ride in this plan. Someone is announcing it the whole way.

The answer is Mordecai. That's the twist. The king says, "Take the robe and the horse to Mordecai the Jew, who is sitting at the king’s gate." (Esther 6:10). Haman walked in with a plan to hang Mordecai. Now he's the one carrying out the honor for him, bakers.

The answer is False. The king says, "Do not neglect anything that you have suggested." (Esther 6:10). The robe, the horse, the parade and the announcement all stay in. Haman doesn't get to cut a single step.

The answer is that Haman cries out the honor announcement. He "paraded him through the city square, crying out before him, 'This is what is done for the man whom the king is delighted to honor!'" (Esther 6:11). He's the one who has to say it. I think that line had to taste strange coming out of his mouth, friends.
The answer is True. "…Mordecai returned to the king’s gate." (Esther 6:12). After the parade, he went back to his spot. The text doesn't tell us what he was thinking, so I won't guess too loudly.
The word is grief. Haman "…rushed home, with his head covered in grief." (Esther 6:12). He had thought the honor was his. Then he cried it out for Mordecai and rushed home hurting, friends.

The answer is that he will surely fall before Mordecai. Zeresh, Haman's wife, and his advisers tell him, "…surely you will fall before him." (Esther 6:13). Haman had told them everything that happened, and that's the word he got back. Friends, that is a hard word to hear.

The answer is Jewish. They say, "Since Mordecai, before whom your downfall has begun, is Jewish, you will not prevail against him…" (Esther 6:13). Their words point to Mordecai being Jewish as the reason. Haman's own household is telling him it's not going his way.

The answer is the banquet Esther prepared. "…the king’s eunuchs arrived and rushed him to the banquet that Esther had prepared." (Esther 6:14). They didn't even let the conversation wrap up. Haman went from one big moment straight to another. And friends, the story isn't over.
